blocks.text: a good day. While this was all fantastic in keeping fit, the biggest benefit from that was that it put me on a 10-mile run loop.
Even as I worked further and further away from home, I found myself making it back to my early years of working in the hospitality industry.
I would have to commute to work, back again, and again, and again.
After a few months of this, I finally came to the conclusion that I wanted to work closer to home, and I had to start to make changes.
For those of you who can afford it, this is easy to say: just move to an area that is closer to work, get a job that is closer to home, or both.
But this is not always the case.
In the past year, I have had to move from London to the Lake District to look after my ailing grandmother, but now I have found myself in a place that has a lot less public transport.
In fact, there is only one bus route that goes near me and that route passes an area where I am not comfortable going on my own.
What do you do when your work is 5 miles away from you and it’s a 10-mile walk to get there?
Well, what about when the 5 miles is 25 or 50 miles?
Working in a remote location like this has presented me with something that I was not aware of.
I am now a commuter. If you work from home, or if you work from a place that is very close to you, I highly suggest that you create a commute.
For me, I do this simply by walking down to a cafe with good WiFi, sitting outside, and enjoying a cup of coffee for about 25 minutes.

blocks.text: you are. Many would argue that reactive mode is the worst way to live.
They’d say we should all be proactive with our lives.
The problem is that some people want to be proactive, but don’t want to put in the work.
A guy who was recently laid off at his job went out of his way to tell everyone he knew that he would be making a six-figure salary this year.
He was confident. It would be his year of making tons of money!
Now, we all know what his outcome is, but at the time, everyone thought he was going to be a rockstar.
But how could he have known that he would suddenly lose his job?
He wasn’t prepared for the situation.
A few months ago, he was in proactive mode.
Now, he’s in reactive mode and is looking for the next opportunity.
We’ve all been through moments like this before.
Life is unpredictable, and our plans change over night.
I think the most important skill to learn is adaptability.
Reacting is not always bad. We need to be ready to react when something unexpected happens in our life.
That doesn’t mean we don’t have control over it.
Reactivity is not a dirty word.
It simply means we have to adapt.
People would like to control everything in their lives and expect the exact same results, even when something unexpected happens.
So what if he suddenly lost his job a month after promising to make big money that year?
What if we were all reactive at times?
Would it make us any less of a human being?
The problem is that he put all of the onus of his financial situation on his own back.
He couldn’t see that this would happen.
No one could have known that he would lose his job.
There are some things out of our control.

blocks.text: a podcast on pragmatism I was worried that it might be a little too abstract, a little too academic.
I was worried that I might fail to connect with folks on a personal level because they didn’t see the value or the “right” way to use their intelligence.
I thought that it might be the kind of thing that you could get a degree in but not necessarily the kind of thing that you could live by.
In that spirit, I’ve decided to make pragmatism personal and accessible in a new weekly audio podcast called the Pragmatism Show.
I want to talk about how we can live with and apply pragmatism in our everyday lives.
But even more than that, I want to talk about how pragmatism impacts and shapes our relationships with others.
I want to explore how to be pragmatic in those relationships, what it means to be a pragmatic person in that respect and also what it means to be a pragmatic philosopher.
I’ve been listening to a number of podcasts over the past few months, and these are the things I’m going to start with when it comes to talking about living a pragmatic life.
Epistemological Pragmatism Epistemology is the philosophy of knowledge.
This is an area that most of us don’t think about very often, and we certainly don’t give a lot of attention to it.
We’ve been in school for most of our lives, and we’re pretty good at it.
We do have a strong sense of what knowledge is and what it means to know something.
We have a very strong sense of what it means to be an authority, and what it means to be an expert.
We have a strong sense of the difference between right and wrong, and we have strong opinions about what we believe is the right thing to do.
But, as a philosopher, I want to question all that.
I want to question my own beliefs.
Why do I believe what I believe?

blocks.text: schedule of writing every other day, editing every other day, and revising every other day.
I wrote in the mornings, took walks during lunchtime, and rewrote at night.
Every other day. (As I said, I was on vacation.)
I wrote a second draft from scratch, then rewrote the entire book a third time.
When it was done, I sent it to the agents.
It was rejected. I had another idea that didn’t pan out, and the deadline came and went.
I got discouraged. But now the agents who rejected my manuscript were the ones rejecting my agents.
That was nearly a year ago, and my latest rejection letter came last week, from an agent who I liked a lot.
She had sent me a request form a few days before, and I had dutifully followed up as soon as the offer was declined.
Now, almost 24 hours later, I had received another rejection letter — this time with a personal note, from someone who I had a personal connection with.
I found out a while ago that she had just been diagnosed with breast cancer, and the story was hard to stomach.
And not in the way you’d think.
I write dark and difficult fiction for adults.
So, when a young girl was diagnosed with cancer, I imagined I might be able to tell her story.
Then, I realized that such a book might be a good way to help her.
Maybe she would feel less alone.
Or, maybe I should say, I imagined her story might be good way to help me.
I imagined it would make me feel more connected to someone.
I imagined I might have a connection to this girl I had never met.

And since Buddhism is a religion that’s deeply concerned with compassion, justice is right there with the three refuges.

When it comes to justice, the term comes up a lot in reference to police misconduct and our criminal justice system, a system that’s plagued by an over incarceration rate and a lack of equitable treatment.
The U.S. ranks first in the world for incarceration.
With so much injustice, where does justice end and injustice begin?
That’s a good question. To me, the beginning of justice starts with people having equal access to resources.
A lack of equitable resources is where a lot of injustice originates, because it’s rooted in the inequality that pervades American society.
The U.S. has the highest incarceration rate of any advanced country in the world.
One reason for this is a racial disparity that affects Black people far more than other people.
When people don’t have the resources they need to survive, such as food, housing, education, and transportation, their lives are in jeopardy.
They are more likely to be arrested and sent to prison instead of getting the help they need.

People who already lack resources, because of things like race and class, can’t afford a lawyer, which means they can’t afford to fight for their freedom, especially when they’ve been arrested for a low-level crime like a traffic infraction or shoplifting.
This can result in a long-term prison sentence.
And those with access to resources have a greater chance of having a good lawyer that can argue their case.
That’s where justice comes into play.
